clue.text: Fine print a delight

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective, delightful; the clue gives a noun phrase

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
an etching is a print made from an etched plate

explanation.surface: Someone admires a finely printed page and calls it a delight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine print' looks like the small text in a contract, but it splits into F for fine and an etching for the print.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fetching is attractive and charming, which is what a delight is, though the answer works as an adjective.

clue.text: Set ALWN = Champion loses round — squashed by Big Daddy

indicators.note: a word that loses something gives it up, so the circle-shaped letter drops out

blocks.note: stray characters in the book's text, padding that plays no part in the wordplay
fat means big or stout
a champion of a cause is its hero
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A wrestling champion loses a bout and is flattened by Big Daddy.
explanation.walkthrough: The book's text opens with stray characters, 'Set ALWN =', that belong to no clue; the clue proper starts at 'Champion'. In a down clue, 'squashed by' puts the champion under the big piece. Big Daddy was a famous British wrestler.
explanation.definitionFit: Daddy is a child's word for a father, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Old slinger, English, bowled in windy Utrecht

indicators.note: windy suggests letters blown about and jumbled, so the place name and its added letters are rearranged

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
b is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled
the Dutch city's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: An old English cricketer is bowled out on a blustery day in the Dutch city of Utrecht.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old slinger' sounds like a veteran bowler, matching the cricket in the surface, but it is a siege engine.
explanation.definitionFit: A trebuchet is a medieval siege engine that hurled stones from a sling on a long throwing arm.

clue.text: Measure causing runner in field to receive shocking treatment

indicators.note: to receive something is to take it inside, so the runner swallows the treatment

blocks.note: a hare is a fast-running animal of open fields
ECT is electroconvulsive therapy, treatment by electric shock

explanation.surface: A runner on the athletics field needs a jolt of emergency treatment.
explanation.definitionFit: A hectare is a metric unit of land area, 10,000 square metres, so it is a measure.

clue.text: In ammunition it replaced explosive component

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of words that follows, across their word breaks

blocks.note: the end of ammunition, then it, then the start of replaced

explanation.surface: It sounds like a history of a new chemical taking the place of an older one in ammunition.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one fact about weapons history; the first word is the signal and the answer runs across 'ammunition it replaced'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitre, or saltpetre, is potassium nitrate, the oxidising ingredient of gunpowder.

clue.text: Compassion from soldiers deployed in temple hospital

indicators.note: troops deployed in a place are stationed inside it, so these soldiers go inside the temple

blocks.note: a wat is a Buddhist temple in Thailand or Cambodia
RM stands for the Royal Marines
H is the map and sign abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: Kindness shown when troops are posted to a hospital housed in a temple.
explanation.definitionFit: Warmth is kindly feeling towards others, a close synonym of compassion.

clue.text: Sceptic is entertained by Hatter, not completely mad

indicators.note: a guest entertained by a host is taken into their home, so this short word goes inside
not completely means not all of it, so the word loses its final letter
mad means crazed or disordered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the word taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A doubter is a guest of the Mad Hatter, who is not quite as mad as he seems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hatter' and 'mad' summon Lewis Carroll's Mad Hatter, but mad is the signal to rearrange the shortened word.
explanation.definitionFit: An atheist disbelieves in God, a particular kind of sceptic about religious claims.

clue.text: Author has knight appear in distance

indicators.note: to appear in something is to be seen inside it, so the knight goes within the distance

blocks.note: a mile is a unit of distance
N is the chess notation for a knight

explanation.surface: A writer gets a knight to make an appearance some way off in the story.
explanation.definitionFit: A. A. Milne wrote the Winnie-the-Pooh books, so he is an author.

clue.text: One on vacation not over the top in making punch

indicators.note: not here means without, so the next two pieces are struck out of the holiday word

blocks.note: a holidaymaker is someone away on holiday
O is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for an over
a lid is the top of a box or jar

explanation.surface: A tourist who stays calm and doesn't go over the top while mixing a bowl of punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the top' looks like the idiom for excessive, but it splits into O for over and LID for the top, and those letters leave the holiday word together. 'Punch' looks like the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A haymaker is a wild, swinging blow with the fist, a type of punch.

clue.text: Bomb outside church planted by sanctimonious tart

indicators.note: one thing outside another wraps around it, so the bomb word surrounds the rest

blocks.note: a mine is a buried bomb
CE is the Church of England
pi is informal British for pious or sanctimonious

explanation.surface: A self-righteous hussy plants a bomb outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tart' looks like an insult to a woman, but it is the pastry. 'Pi' is British school slang for pious or holier-than-thou.
explanation.definitionFit: A mince pie is a small British Christmas tart filled with spiced dried fruit called mincemeat.

clue.text: With husband in supermarket, this aptly represented 25 ac

indicators.note: with a person inside a shop means that person is placed within its name
to represent something afresh is to present it again in a new form, so these letters are recast

blocks.note: H is the standard abbreviation for husband
Tesco is Britain's biggest supermarket chain
the letters of these two words, taken as written

explanation.surface: A wife shopping with her husband sees the scene as a fitting picture of the play at 25 across.
explanation.walkthrough: 25 across is MACBETH. Theatre people avoid saying its name aloud backstage and use this phrase instead; 'aptly' looks like part of the surface but is anagram fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre superstition says the name of Shakespeare's Macbeth brings bad luck, so actors use this euphemism instead.

clue.text: Train ferries coin between terminals at Stoke and Carlisle

indicators.note: the terminals of a line are its end stations, so each place name gives only its final letter
to ferry something is to carry it, so the two end letters carry the coin between them

blocks.note: the final letter of Stoke
a ducat was a gold coin used across Europe
the final letter of Carlisle

explanation.surface: A railway service carries money from one end of the line to the other, Stoke to Carlisle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' looks like a railway train, but it is the verb meaning to teach. Stoke and Carlisle are English cities on the West Coast main line.
explanation.definitionFit: To train someone is to teach them a skill, which is what educating them means.

clue.text: Lion-headed monster to agree with hawk-headed god

blocks.note: to chime with something is to agree or match with it
Ra, the Egyptian sun god, was shown with a falcon's head

explanation.surface: Two creatures from mythology, one with a lion's head and one with a hawk's, sit side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Chimera was a fire-breathing monster with a lion's head, a goat's body and a serpent's tail.

clue.text: Verges in Eastbridge paid to board vessel — Suffolk submerged here?

indicators.note: the verges of a road are its edges, so only the outside letters of each word are kept
to board a ship is to go inside it, so these letters go into the vessel

blocks.note: a ship is a sea-going vessel
the first and last letters of Eastbridge
the first and last letters of paid

explanation.surface: Church officials in a Suffolk village pay their way onto a boat, and the county seems to sink.
explanation.walkthrough: The scan reads 'Vergers', but the wordplay needs 'Verges', the edges of each word. Suffolk is a breed of sheep as well as an English county, and Eastbridge is a Suffolk village.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheep dip is a bath of insecticide that sheep are plunged into, so a Suffolk sheep would be submerged in one.

clue.text: Greek character celebrated in return, having set off

indicators.note: in return means coming back the other way, so the combined letters are read backwards

blocks.note: eta is the seventh letter of the Greek alphabet
noted means famous or celebrated

explanation.surface: A famous Greek is fêted on his homecoming after leaving on a journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' looks like starting a journey, which fits the return in the surface, but it means to explode a bomb.
explanation.definitionFit: To detonate a charge is to set it off, making it explode.

clue.text: Sporting supporter holds record in home of the brave

indicators.note: something that holds an item has it inside, so the record sits within the supporter

blocks.note: a golf tee holds the ball up before the drive
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A sports fan clutches a record at a stadium in America, land of the free and home of the brave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home of the brave' recalls the US anthem, but a brave here is a Native American warrior.
explanation.definitionFit: A tepee is the cone-shaped tent of Plains peoples, so it is literally a dwelling for a Native American brave.

clue.text: Tried with Conservative to answer Liberal French citizen

blocks.note: something tried and tested is proven
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
A is the abbreviation for answer
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A French voter weighs up the Conservative and Liberal candidates.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Liberal French' sound like a political leaning, but Liberal is a lone L.
explanation.definitionFit: A Provençal is a native or inhabitant of Provence in southern France, so one kind of French citizen.

clue.text: Pot allows one to be free from pain under cheek

indicators.note: to be free from something is to be rid of it, so the letter for one leaves the word
in a down clue a piece under another is written below it, so the cheek word comes first and this one second

blocks.note: sauce is cheekiness or impudence
taken as written
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Smoking pot lets a user forget the pain of a sore cheek.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pot' looks like cannabis, but it is the kitchen sense. In a down clue, 'under cheek' puts the shortened pain below SAUCE.
explanation.definitionFit: A saucepan is a deep cooking pot with a handle.

clue.text: Soon is about time for this man

indicators.note: about means around here, so one word goes round the letter for time

blocks.note: anon is an old word for soon
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone says it will soon be this man's turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Anton is a man's first name, which is all that the vague 'this man' asks for.

clue.text: Write uplifting melody for part of musical work

indicators.note: in a down clue uplifting means raised from bottom to top, so the writing word is read upwards

blocks.note: to pen is to write
a tune is a melody

explanation.surface: A composer writes a rousing melody for one movement of a larger work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uplifting' looks like a description of the melody, but it reverses only the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Neptune is the last movement of Holst's orchestral suite The Planets, so it is one part of a musical work.

clue.text: Alpine heroine in child's book

indicators.note: a heroine placed in something sits inside it, so her name goes within the child

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
Heidi is the Swiss mountain girl of Johanna Spyri's story

explanation.surface: A mountain heroine appears in a children's storybook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child's book' looks like a description of Heidi's own story, but the child is the outer wrapper and the book is the definition, THE IDIOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Idiot is a novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky, so it is an example of a book.

clue.text: Say no to failure

blocks.note: first meaning: to refuse an offer politely
second meaning: a gradual worsening or weakening

explanation.surface: Advice to refuse to accept defeat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as one phrase, rejecting failure, but it is two separate senses of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Decline is a verb for turning something down and a noun for a falling off in health, strength or fortune.

clue.text: Getting closer to pheasant in hunting land is simple

indicators.note: the closer of something is what finishes it, so only the final letter of the bird is used
getting in here means entering, so that letter goes into the hunting ground

blocks.note: a chase is an area of unenclosed land kept for hunting
the final letter of pheasant

explanation.surface: Stalking up close to a pheasant on a hunting estate turns out to be easy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting closer to' reads as stalking the bird, but closer means the bird's last letter. A chase is an old British term for a hunting ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste can mean plain and unadorned in style, as in simple, restrained design.

clue.text: Study about swindle produces article that's spiked

indicators.note: about means around here, so the study word goes around the swindle

blocks.note: to con is an old word for to study or learn by heart
a ramp is British slang for a swindle or racket

explanation.surface: An investigation into fraud yields a newspaper article that the editor spikes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spiked' suggests a news story that is killed off, but here it means fitted with spikes.
explanation.definitionFit: A crampon is a metal frame with spikes strapped to a boot for climbing on ice.

clue.text: Lucky creature, heading off for prestigious meeting

indicators.note: with its heading off, the word loses its first letter

blocks.note: a mascot is an animal or figure kept to bring luck

explanation.surface: A team's lucky animal sets off for a grand gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: Ascot is a racecourse near Windsor whose royal race meeting each June is a high point of the English social season.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal Ascot is a race meeting famed for royalty, top hats and high society, so it is a prestigious event.

clue.text: Mother caught with Hebrew character in bloody drama

blocks.note: ma is an informal word for mother
c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
beth is the second letter of the Hebrew alphabet

explanation.surface: A mother is caught up with a Jewish character in a gory stage play.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Macbeth is a tragedy full of murder, and its hero's ambition leaves a trail of blood.

clue.text: Nonsense marks end to scholarly attention

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for the mark, the old German currency
the final letter of scholarly
to give something your eye is to pay attention to it

explanation.surface: A teacher's marks put an end to a pupil's interest in scholarship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My eye!' is an old British exclamation of disbelief, meaning rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: As an exclamation the phrase dismisses a claim as rubbish, the same as saying nonsense.

clue.text: Salvage relationship — and what's left of crockery!

blocks.note: first meaning: to rebuild things after a break-up or disaster
second meaning: literally gathering up the bits of broken plates

explanation.surface: After a row, a couple try to save things, and there is broken china on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads literally: the shards of smashed crockery are the pieces, and you pick them up.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means restoring normal life after a setback, taken from clearing up something that has been smashed.

clue.text: Eccentric person for example gets married in tree

blocks.note: a nut is slang for a crazy or eccentric person
M is the standard abbreviation for married
e.g. is the abbreviation for 'for example'

explanation.surface: An oddball gets married up a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets married' attaches the marriage letter to the front of the example abbreviation, so it comes before it rather than after.
explanation.definitionFit: The nutmeg is a tropical evergreen whose seed is ground as the spice of the same name.

clue.text: Troops at glen heard bugle call

indicators.note: something heard is taken in by ear, so the words are judged by their sound rather than spelling

blocks.note: RE stands for the Royal Engineers
a glen is a narrow valley in Scotland

explanation.surface: Soldiers camped in a Scottish glen hear the bugle sound.
explanation.walkthrough: Said the British way, re-VAL-ee, the call sounds like RE plus valley.
explanation.definitionFit: Reveille is the bugle call played at dawn to wake soldiers.
